title: White v. Corlies & Tifft
lead: A builder buys lumber and begins work after merchants invite him to fit out their offices. When they withdraw the proposal, his damages claim turns on whether those private preparations communicated acceptance.

actors.name: White
actors.role: New York builder seeking damages for the countermanded office project.

actors.name: Corlies and his associates
actors.role: Merchants negotiating to have offices at 57 Broadway fitted up.

proceedings: A jury found for White after an instruction permitting acceptance by commencing the job without indicating assent to the merchants.
The Court of Appeals reversed and ordered a new trial, with costs to abide the event.
limits: This account follows the canonical historical brief without a fresh audit. Black-walnut, white-pine, and timing details are explicitly attributed to the casebook’s account of appellate-record testimony. The reported September 30 reference apparently concerns the September 29 note. Later Restatement provisions and hypothetical different conduct are not 1871 holdings.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent primary-source audit claimed.

sections.title: The merchants seek an estimate but leave agreement incomplete
paragraphs: White operated a building business on Fortieth Street in New York City. Corlies, Tifft, and their associates did business on Dey Street and wanted offices at 57 Broadway fitted up. In September 1865, they supplied specifications and requested an estimate.

The casebook’s account of White’s appellate-record testimony adds that the merchants first wanted black-walnut work completed in twenty-one days. White said he could not finish that hardwood work in that period, so they sought an estimate for white pine. His September 28 estimate stated no completion time.

After receiving that estimate, the merchants were to consider it and communicate their decision. They changed the specifications that day and sent the revisions for White’s assent under his estimate. He signed and returned them. That assent to revised specifications was part of negotiations; it did not itself complete the whole bargain.

sources.pinpoint: 46 N.Y. 467–469; assigned editorial record notes at printed 223

sections.title: The bookkeeper’s note prompts uncommunicated preparations
sections.cue: What did White do before the countermand?
paragraphs: The merchants’ bookkeeper sent a September 29 note saying that, upon an agreement to finish the offices within two weeks from that date, White could begin at once. The writer added that he would probably call again between five and six that afternoon.

White sent no reply. Immediately after receiving the note, he bought lumber and began working on it. The lumber was suitable for other comparable jobs, and the work resembled work he would do for those jobs. The merchants countermanded the proposal the next day. According to the casebook’s account of the record, that countermand requested another estimate for black walnut.

White claimed his conduct had accepted the undertaking before withdrawal and sued for damages. The published opinion once calls the relevant communication a September 30 note; the casebook identifies that as an apparent reference to the September 29 note.

sources.pinpoint: 46 N.Y. 467–470; assigned editorial notes at printed 223

sections.title: The jury is allowed to find acceptance from commencement alone
sections.cue: What legal error did the merchants preserve?
paragraphs: The trial judge instructed that White did not need to return to the merchants and say he had begun; he could act on their note and commence the job. The merchants excepted to that instruction. The jury found for White, and the General Term of the First Judicial District affirmed.

On appeal, the Court of Appeals had to decide whether White’s decision and preparations were enough when they had neither communicated assent nor put it into an appropriate course of communication. Justice Folger treated the note as an offer needing acceptance and found no earlier completed contract in the evidence or jury findings.

sections.title: The Court of Appeals requires an objectively communicative act
sections.cue: Why did these preparations fail although receipt is not always necessary?
paragraphs: When parties are apart, acceptance requires an appropriate outward act. The offeror need not invariably know of it before formation, but it must be placed in a proper course of communication so that it ordinarily will reach the offeror within a reasonable time. A mailed acceptance illustrates the difference: dispatch can complete a contract before delivery because the offeree has taken a communicative step.

White’s generic lumber purchases and work did not identify this undertaking as the one accepted. His intention could explain those acts privately, but could not give the merchants an outward indication of assent. Nothing communicated acceptance, set communication in motion, or necessarily would result in communication. His expenditures and labor established preparation, not the required acceptance.

The permission to begin immediately supplied White’s strongest position: an instruction to start could invite responsive conduct. The court nevertheless focused on what his actual acts manifested. It did not forbid acceptance by conduct or require actual receipt of notice in every case. Nor did it decide whether work at the specified offices or another unequivocal act directed to this project would suffice.

sections.title: A new trial follows, leaving broader formulations for later law
paragraphs: On November 20, 1871, the Court of Appeals reversed and ordered a new trial, with costs depending on the ultimate outcome. The justices concurred, with Justice Allen not voting. The court did not enter a final damages award for either side.

The note’s opening phrase might require assent to the new deadline before commencement or might authorize commencement as responsive conduct; the court did not comprehensively resolve every reading. Its result remained tied to White’s uncommunicated work on general-purpose materials.

Later Restatement provisions organize related questions differently: § 62 addresses beginning invited performance as acceptance with a promise to complete, § 45 protects beginning performance where only completed performance is invited, and §§ 54 and 56 address notice. Those later frameworks still require distinguishing requested performance from preparation, but the 1871 court did not apply them.

sources.pinpoint: 46 N.Y. 469–470; assigned editorial Notes at printed 224–225
